lighting.title: Open Shade Portrait
lighting.text: Place the subject in open shade with a broad, unobstructed view of the sky acting as a large natural softbox. Keep the face evenly illuminated, retain gentle directional modeling from the brighter side of the sky, and protect accurate skin and product color. Use a subtly brighter background or edge separation without direct-sun hotspots, harsh eye sockets, or mixed color temperatures.

lighting.title: Window Light with Negative Fill
lighting.text: Use a large side window as the key light, softened by diffusion, with negative fill on the shadow side to create controlled sculptural contrast. Preserve a smooth transition from highlight to shadow, clean catchlights, and readable material texture. Keep the far side of the face and product detailed rather than crushed, with no competing practical lights or accidental color casts.

lighting.title: Overcast Color Accuracy
lighting.text: Use bright overcast daylight for soft, even illumination with controlled highlights and clear product color. Retain gentle facial shape and visible texture while avoiding flat gray rendering; add subtle directional separation through the subject's position relative to the sky. The final result should feel natural, clean, and commercially reliable, with no blue skin cast or dull material finish.

lighting.title: Sunset Rim with Fill
lighting.text: Backlight the subject with low golden-hour sun to create a warm rim around hair, fabric, or product contours, then use soft frontal fill to retain face and product detail. Expose for luminous highlights without clipping the sky or turning the subject into a silhouette. Keep the warm atmosphere intentional while preserving believable skin tone and the true product color.

lighting.title: Graphic Hard Sun
lighting.text: Use direct high-contrast sunlight as a graphic design element: crisp, intentional shadows; clear geometric shapes; and a defined highlight pattern across the scene. Position the subject so key facial features and product details remain readable. Preserve exposure in the brightest areas and deep shadow detail where needed; avoid accidental squinting, cluttered shadows, or a washed-out midday look.

lighting.title: Beauty Clamshell Studio
lighting.text: Light with a large soft key above and slightly in front of the subject, supported by a low frontal reflector or fill. Create clean eye catchlights, flattering under-chin fill, smooth skin transitions, and accurate product rendering. Retain pores, fine hair, and material micro-texture; avoid flatness, plastic retouching, hard nose shadows, and specular glare on glossy surfaces.

lighting.title: Motivated Practical Night
lighting.text: Build a believable night scene motivated by visible practical sources such as lamps, signs, windows, or streetlights. Let each light source explain the direction and color of illumination on the subject, with a controlled key preserving essential detail. Use contrast and pools of light for atmosphere while avoiding random neon spill, noisy blacks, clipped bulbs, or lighting that ignores the visible set.

poses.title: Natural Weight Shift
poses.text: Use a relaxed standing pose with weight settled naturally into one leg, a soft bend in the opposite knee, shoulders released, and the torso turned slightly away from camera. Keep the neck long, hands purposeful but loose, and the expression calm and present. The pose should create a believable S-curve and show the garment or product silhouette without stiffness or exaggerated fashion posing.

poses.title: Walking Arrival
poses.text: Capture a natural mid-stride arrival: one foot grounded, the other moving forward, arms responding softly to the walk, gaze directed toward the destination or an off-camera point. Maintain believable balance, cloth movement, and a relaxed face. Leave visual space ahead of the subject to support the direction of travel and avoid frozen limbs, duplicated feet, or runway-like exaggeration unless requested.

poses.title: Seated Conversation
poses.text: Pose the subject seated with a grounded posture, one natural point of support, relaxed shoulders, and hands engaged with a meaningful object or conversational gesture. Turn the torso slightly rather than facing squarely forward; let the expression suggest an unguarded moment of listening, thinking, or speaking. Keep legs, hands, and furniture contact physically plausible and avoid a rigid catalog pose.

poses.title: Purposeful Product Interaction
poses.text: Show the product being used through a simple, credible action that reveals its intended scale, feature, and value. Position hands so fingers remain anatomically clear and never cover key branding, construction, or interface details. Make the gaze, posture, and grip support the action; the interaction should feel observed in real life rather than staged solely for the camera.

poses.title: Over-Shoulder Lookback
poses.text: Turn the body three-quarters away from camera, then bring the face back over the nearer shoulder with a relaxed chin and natural neck line. Use the shoulder and garment structure to create depth while keeping both eyes, facial proportions, and key product details visible. The expression should feel like an authentic pause in movement, not an extreme twist.

poses.title: Grounded Power Stance
poses.text: Use a balanced, grounded stance with feet set naturally beneath the body, an upright spine, relaxed jaw, and open chest. Keep arms either at ease or engaged in one purposeful gesture, with no clenched or awkward hands. The pose should communicate confidence through stillness, proportion, and direct intention—not through exaggerated aggression or distorted perspective.

poses.title: Detail-Revealing Gesture
poses.text: Use a restrained hand or body gesture that directs attention to a specific product feature, texture, closure, or material detail. Keep fingertips separated and natural, pressure believable, and the gesture secondary to the feature it reveals. Frame the action so the viewer can understand both the object and the tactile relationship without occlusion or confusing overlaps.

shots.title: Narrative Establishing Wide
shots.text: Begin with a wide establishing shot that clearly locates the subject in an environment and introduces the story world. Keep the subject readable against the background, preserve a distinct focal path, and include only environmental details that add context. Use foreground, middle ground, and background with deliberate depth; avoid making the subject too small or letting set clutter overwhelm the narrative.

shots.title: Medium Action Shot
shots.text: Frame the subject from approximately waist or thigh up while they perform one clear action. Balance facial expression, body language, and meaningful surroundings so the viewer can understand who is acting and what is happening. Keep hands and the relevant product interaction in frame, with enough space in the action direction to make the shot feel natural.

shots.title: Emotion Close-Up
shots.text: Use a close-up that prioritizes the eyes, expression, and a small meaningful detail. Focus critically on the nearer eye or intended product feature, use depth of field with restraint, and retain enough skin or material texture for realism. Crop with intention—never through an awkward joint or essential feature—and keep the background unobtrusive.

shots.title: Over-the-Shoulder Context
shots.text: Frame over the subject's shoulder to connect the viewer to what they are seeing, making, choosing, or using. Keep the shoulder as a soft foreground anchor, the point of attention sharp and legible, and the composition free of obstructive overlap. The shot should feel like a participant's perspective while still clearly communicating the relevant action or product.

shots.title: Macro Evidence Shot
shots.text: Create a macro detail shot that acts as proof of quality: isolate the weave, grain, stitching, finish, ingredient, interface, or craftsmanship detail that supports the claim. Use shallow depth only where it helps, keep the critical plane of detail sharply resolved, and control reflections and highlights so the material remains recognizable rather than abstract.

shots.title: First-Person Participation
shots.text: Use a first-person point of view that makes the audience feel physically present in the interaction. Include only the necessary hands, tools, or foreground cues to establish participation, then lead the eye to the action or product. Keep scale, hand anatomy, perspective, and contact believable; do not let the POV become a confusing wide-angle distortion.

shots.title: Detail Reveal Push-In
shots.text: Start on a composed wider view, then make one smooth, motivated push-in toward the most meaningful face, product feature, or action detail. Keep the move slow enough to feel intentional and preserve focus throughout. End on a stable, readable composition that rewards the reveal; avoid sudden acceleration, focus hunting, or changes to identity, product details, or lighting during the move.

compositions.title: Foreground Depth Triangle
compositions.text: Build depth with a subtle foreground element, a clearly readable subject in the middle ground, and a simplified background that reinforces place. Arrange the three planes so they create a directional triangle leading back to the subject. Keep foreground blur or occlusion controlled; it should add immersion and scale without blocking faces, product details, or the main action.

compositions.title: Gaze & Action Direction
compositions.text: Place the subject off-center with enough open space in the direction of their gaze, movement, or gesture. Use that space to imply a destination, thought, or incoming action, while maintaining a clean focal relationship between subject and environment. Keep the crop and balance deliberate; avoid trapping the subject against the frame edge or leaving empty space without narrative purpose.

compositions.title: Frame Within a Frame
compositions.text: Use an archway, doorway, window, foliage, shelving, or other environmental structure to create a secondary frame around the subject. Preserve a clean visual opening, clear subject separation, and believable scale. The surrounding frame should deepen context and direct attention inward, not create clutter, tangencies, or distracting dark edges around the subject.

compositions.title: Layered Asymmetry
compositions.text: Create an intentionally asymmetric composition by balancing unequal visual weights: a dominant subject or color mass on one side, countered by a smaller detail, line, light source, or negative-space field on the other. Use layers and directional lines to keep the frame active while protecting a single clear focal point. The imbalance should feel designed, not accidental.

compositions.title: Repetition with a Break
compositions.text: Use repeated forms, colors, objects, or gestures to establish visual rhythm, then introduce one meaningful variation that becomes the focal point. Keep spacing and perspective coherent enough for the pattern to read immediately. The break should communicate the story, product, or idea—not feel like an unintentional duplicate or rendering error.

compositions.title: Reflection & Duality
compositions.text: Compose the subject with a credible reflection in a mirror, window, polished surface, or water, using the reflected view to reveal a complementary angle, emotion, or detail. Align perspective, light, scale, and contact with the reflective surface accurately. Let the reflection enrich the narrative while keeping the primary subject unmistakably clear.

compositions.title: Knolling Information System
compositions.text: Arrange related objects in a precise overhead grid with consistent spacing, clear alignment, and purposeful orientation. Use a simple surface, controlled soft light, and minimal shadows to make every item legible. Establish hierarchy through scale and grouping, while retaining a practical sense of how the objects relate rather than making the layout feel randomly decorative.

cameras.title: Eye-Level Observer
cameras.text: Use an eye-level camera position with a natural observer's perspective. Keep verticals stable, facial proportions undistorted, and the relationship between subject and environment believable. This viewpoint should make the viewer feel present with the subject rather than looking down on or up at them, making it ideal for honest portraiture, product use, and documentary storytelling.

cameras.title: Controlled Low-Angle Hero
cameras.text: Place the camera slightly below the subject's eyeline to add confidence and scale while keeping the lens far enough back to protect natural proportions. Use clean verticals, a controlled horizon, and an uncluttered sky or architectural background. The perspective should feel aspirational and grounded, never distorted, domineering, or accidental.

cameras.title: High-Angle Observation
cameras.text: Use a gently elevated camera angle to reveal the subject's activity, surrounding objects, or spatial relationship. Keep the angle shallow enough to preserve believable body proportions and facial connection. Use it to create intimacy, organization, or a sense of watching a real moment unfold—not a surveillance or diminutive effect.

cameras.title: True Overhead Precision
cameras.text: Position the camera precisely perpendicular to the surface for a true overhead view. Keep edges and grid lines square to the frame, scale consistent across objects, and light soft enough to preserve color and surface detail. Use this camera position for flat lays, process steps, ingredients, or object systems where clear comparison and arrangement matter.

cameras.title: Shoulder-Height Tracking
cameras.text: Track alongside or just behind the subject at shoulder height with a smooth, human-paced movement. Keep framing stable enough to read facial expression, body language, and product interaction while allowing the environment to pass naturally. The camera should feel like an attentive companion, with no mechanical jitter, sudden reframing, or unexplained speed changes.

cameras.title: Through-Object Observer
cameras.text: Photograph through a nearby object—such as glass, foliage, a doorway, fabric, or shelving—to create a sense of discovery and depth. Keep the subject's essential features and product details unobstructed, control reflections and flare, and make the foreground feel like an intentional point of view rather than an accidental blockage.

cameras.title: Static Tableau
cameras.text: Lock the camera into a composed static frame and let the subject, environment, or light create the movement within it. Establish a strong visual hierarchy before action begins, then hold the framing long enough for small gestures and details to register. Maintain stable geometry and exposure; use this approach for deliberate, art-directed storytelling rather than inactive coverage.

lenses.title: 24mm Environmental Wide
lenses.text: Use a 24mm wide-angle perspective to place the subject decisively within an expansive environment. Keep the camera level and give the subject adequate distance from the lens to protect body and product proportions. Let foreground-to-background depth communicate scale and place, while avoiding stretched faces, bowed architecture, or meaningless empty surroundings.

lenses.title: 35mm Intimate Context
lenses.text: Use a 35mm perspective for an intimate environmental view that includes meaningful context without looking excessively wide. Position the camera close enough for immediacy while keeping facial and product proportions natural. This lens language should feel present, contemporary, and documentary-minded, with clear subject separation and no edge distortion on important features.

lenses.title: 50mm Human Perspective
lenses.text: Use a 50mm normal-lens perspective for balanced, believable spatial relationships. Frame portraits, products, and interactions with natural proportions, moderate background context, and a calm observational feel. Use selective focus only when it supports the story; retain enough depth to show the setting and make product scale or use understandable.

lenses.title: 85mm Portrait Separation
lenses.text: Use an 85mm portrait perspective to give the face and product a flattering, calm compression while separating the subject from the background. Keep the camera far enough away for a relaxed expression and natural posture, then use the longer focal length to simplify distracting surroundings. Focus precisely on the eyes or critical product feature and retain tactile detail.

lenses.title: 105mm Detail Compression
lenses.text: Use a 105mm perspective for refined detail studies, compressed environmental layers, or premium product close-ups. Isolate the chosen feature with controlled background separation while preserving accurate dimensions, texture, and edge detail. Avoid overly thin focus planes that make important construction details disappear; the shot should feel precise and luxurious, not merely blurred.

lenses.title: 90mm Macro Proof
lenses.text: Use a 90mm macro perspective to document fine workmanship, surface texture, ingredients, or interfaces at close range. Maintain a stable focus plane exactly where the evidence lies, use soft directional light to reveal relief and grain, and preserve realistic scale cues. Do not exaggerate defects or turn a material study into an unrecognizable abstract pattern.

lenses.title: Telephoto Layering
lenses.text: Use a longer telephoto perspective to compress distant planes into elegant visual layers, making light, architecture, foliage, or crowd texture support the subject. Keep the subject clearly separated through tonal contrast and focus, and make the compressed space feel intentional. Avoid flattening the story so much that the environment loses meaning or scale becomes confusing.

environments.title: Sunlit Working Atelier
environments.text: Set the scene in a calm working atelier with tall diffuse windows, a few purposeful tools or samples, honest material surfaces, and room for the subject to work or pause naturally. Use warm neutral tones, soft directional daylight, and an orderly but lived-in composition. Every object should support a story of making, design, or care; avoid generic clutter and overly staged workshop props.

environments.title: Modernist Courtyard
environments.text: Place the subject in a modernist courtyard defined by clean planes, textured stone or plaster, architectural shadow, a small amount of sculptural greenery, and generous negative space. Use the geometry to frame the subject and create graphic depth while retaining a human scale. Keep surfaces believable, uncluttered, and free from unrelated luxury clichés.

environments.title: Neighborhood Grocery
environments.text: Set the story in a specific, welcoming neighborhood grocery with hand-lettered signs, seasonal produce, practical shelving, and authentic local details. Use an observational perspective, believable fluorescent or window-mixed light corrected for natural skin tone, and product placement that respects the real space. The environment should feel community-rooted rather than like a generic supermarket set.

environments.title: Rainy Window Café
environments.text: Create an intimate café interior beside a rain-speckled window, with soft reflected daylight, warm practical lamps, subtle steam, and a restrained city background beyond the glass. Frame the subject with natural table objects and reflections that enrich the mood without obscuring expression or product detail. Keep rainfall, glass, and lighting physically plausible and avoid excessive moody darkness.

environments.title: Blue-Hour Rooftop
environments.text: Use a believable rooftop at blue hour with a layered city skyline, fading ambient sky light, practical building glow, and enough foreground texture to anchor the subject. Balance cool ambient light with controlled warm accents so skin, product color, and silhouette remain readable. Keep the skyline recognizable as depth rather than turning it into a noisy field of random lights.

environments.title: Lived-In Home Entryway
environments.text: Set an everyday arrival or departure in a thoughtfully lived-in home entryway: natural daylight, a practical bench or hook, personal but non-identifying objects, tactile flooring, and visual order with a little real-life imperfection. Use the setting to support an action—putting something down, leaving, returning, or preparing—without crowding the frame or relying on generic staged décor.

environments.title: Coastal Wind Landscape
environments.text: Place the subject in a windswept coastal landscape with textured grass, weathered stone, open sky, and a distant horizon. Let the wind subtly affect hair, fabric, and nearby foliage to create credible motion, while using soft directional daylight to keep skin and product color true. Avoid an overdramatic storm, empty postcard scenery, or environmental elements that compete with the subject.
